1	# Carbon-aware Compute Scheduling Market
2	
3	A backend service for a carbon-aware batch-compute scheduling market. The service will evolve around scheduling and migrating batch jobs using live energy mix, regional carbon intensity, execution cost, deadlines, and data-residency constraints.
4	
5	## Run
6	
7	Requires Python 3.11 or newer and has no third-party runtime dependencies.
8	
9	```bash
10	python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
11	```
12	
13	The initial public endpoint is `GET /health`, which returns JSON with `status: "ok"`.
14	
15	## Audit endpoint
16	
17	```bash
18	python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --audit PATH --token TOKEN
19	```
20	
21	`--audit` and `--token` form a pair: both omitted leaves `GET /audit` a plain 404 like any other unknown path, while giving only one, an empty value or a repeated option is a usage error (exit status 2). When both are given, `GET /audit` serves read-only queries against the audit journal at `PATH`; clients cannot select another file.
22	
23	Requests must carry exactly one `X-Audit-Token` header whose value equals `TOKEN` (missing, blank or duplicated headers get 401, a mismatched value 403). The query string maps to `audit.search`: optional `cursor`, `limit` (a decimal integer from 1 to 1000, default 100), `op`, `stage` and `key` filters. Unknown, repeated or empty parameters get 400 `invalid_request`. A missing journal gets 404 `audit_not_found`, malformed journal content 409 `audit_invalid`, and other I/O failures 503 `audit_unavailable`.
24	
25	## Multi-token scoped authorization
26	
27	```bash
28	python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --audit PATH --auth CONFIG
29	```
30	
31	`--auth` is an alternative to `--token`; the two are mutually exclusive, and enabling the audit endpoint requires exactly one of them (anything else is a usage error, exit status 2). `CONFIG` is a UTF-8 file whose every non-empty line is a six-element JSON array:
32	
33	```json
34	["name", "sha256-hex", grace_until, ops, stages, keys]
35	```
36	
37	- `name` — a unique non-empty label for the token.
38	- `sha256-hex` — the lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 of the token's raw UTF-8 bytes; unique across records. The file never holds plaintext tokens.
39	- `grace_until` — `null` or a non-negative integer Unix second; the token stays valid while the current Unix second is not greater than it.
40	- `ops`, `stages`, `keys` — each either `"*"` (the filter may be omitted or take any legal value) or an array of distinct non-empty strings, in which case the request must carry that filter explicitly with a value in the array. Operation and stage scopes use the search filter domains (`copy`/`restore`; `成功`, `校验`, `执行`, `同步`, `回滚`); history keys match exactly.
41	
42	The whole file is validated at startup (any error exits with status 2 without listening) and re-read on every request, so a same-directory atomic replacement rotates tokens without a restart: add the new digest and set a grace cutoff on the old one. A configuration that cannot be read or validated after startup answers 503 `auth_unavailable`. Unknown or expired tokens get 403; a valid token whose request lacks a required in-scope filter gets 403 as well, after query-parameter validation (400) and before the audit file is ever opened.
43	
44	## Proof export endpoint
45	
46	```bash
47	python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --audit PATH --token TOKEN --checkpoint CPATH
48	```
49	
50	`--checkpoint` enables `GET /audit/proof`, the online export of `audit_proof.export` against the fixed checkpoint `CPATH`; it may only be given together with `--audit` (alone, empty or repeated it is a usage error, exit status 2). Without it the proof path stays a plain 404 like any other unknown path. Clients can never select the audit or checkpoint file through the query.
51	
52	The same authorization as `GET /audit` applies, in the same order (401/403, 400 `invalid_request`, scoped filters 403, 503 `auth_unavailable`). The query takes a mandatory non-empty `generation` name, an optional `final` flag (exactly `true` or `false`, defaulting to `false`) and the usual `cursor`, `limit`, `op`, `stage` and `key` filters. A successful export answers 200 with the offline-savable proof object, its page computed from the same journal snapshot the proof seals. The proof object is version 2 and ends with `checkpoint_etag`: the strong entity tag of the checkpoint's raw bytes after this export's anchor commit — one double-quoted string of 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, the SHA-256 of the complete bytes, exactly the computation and quoting the checkpoint download serves — so every proof is bound to precisely one checkpoint snapshot, and any later anchor, closing or new generation rebinds the proofs that follow it. A missing journal or checkpoint parent directory gets 404 `proof_not_found` (the real paths never leak); an invalid chain, checkpoint, generation state or growth relation gets 409 `proof_invalid` and appends no anchor; locking or I/O failures get 503 `proof_unavailable` with the old checkpoint preserved.
53	
54	## Checkpoint snapshot endpoint
55	
56	With `--checkpoint` configured, `GET /audit/checkpoint` offers the fixed checkpoint file itself as a read-only, conditionally cached download. The endpoint takes no path or query parameters: the response always comes from the one `CPATH` fixed at startup, so a client can neither select nor probe a location.
57	
58	Authorization follows the same order as the other audit endpoints: a missing, blank or duplicated `X-Audit-Token` is 401 `unauthorized`; an unknown or expired token is 403 `forbidden`; an authorization configuration that cannot be read or validated at request time is 503 `auth_unavailable` with no configuration detail in the body. A multi-token record may download only when its operation, stage and history-key scopes are all `*`; any restricted scope gets 403.
59	
60	The optional `If-None-Match` header may be omitted or appear exactly once as a single strong tag — one double-quoted string of 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits. A blank, duplicated or malformed conditional header gets 400 `invalid_request` and never opens the checkpoint; the same goes for any query string. The response on success (200) is the checkpoint's original UTF-8 bytes, served verbatim with `Content-Type: application/json` — never re-serialized — and an `ETag` that is the lowercase SHA-256 of the complete response bytes in strong-tag form (`"<64 hex>"`). When the conditional value equals the current ETag the answer is 304 with an empty body and the same ETag; otherwise it is 200 with the full bytes, and both decisions are made from one validated snapshot.
61	
62	The bytes are read under the same checkpoint lock exports use (shared), held from open through validation and ETag computation, so a request racing an export observes only a complete old or complete new version. A missing checkpoint gets 404 `checkpoint_not_found`; bytes that are not valid UTF-8 or JSON, or a checkpoint with an illegal version, field order, anchor or digest chain, get 409 `checkpoint_invalid` with a body of only `{"error":...}`; other I/O failures get 503 `checkpoint_unavailable`. Real paths and system messages never appear in an error. Without `--checkpoint` the path remains a plain 404 like any other unknown path.
63	
64	## Offline bundle verification
65	
66	```bash
67	python -m carbon_market verify-bundle --checkpoint CPATH --proof PPATH --etag ETAG [--trust-dir PATH]
68	```
69	
70	`verify-bundle` verifies a downloaded checkpoint/proof pair entirely offline; it never touches the journal and never rewrites its inputs. All three mandatory options must appear exactly once with non-empty values, and `--etag` must be a single strong tag — one double-quoted string of 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, exactly as the download's `ETag` header carried it. Any argument or tag-format error exits with status 2 and `{"error":"invalid_request"}` on stderr before either file is read.
71	
72	Verification first recomputes the tag from the checkpoint's raw bytes — a mismatch fails immediately — then reads both files as UTF-8 JSON (negative-zero and non-finite number literals are format errors), revalidates the checkpoint's complete anchor chain, and applies the same offline proof checks as `audit_proof.verify`: embedded log bytes, query parameters, recomputed page, cursor and root digest, with the generation, anchor and closed state taken from the checkpoint snapshot in hand. The passed `--etag`, the recomputed tag and the proof's bound `checkpoint_etag` must all three agree, so an old proof against a new checkpoint, a new proof against an old checkpoint, or a tag carried by another download response is a verification failure. Proofs without the snapshot binding (version 1) are not verifiable offline and count as incomplete proof structures. Everything happens under the checkpoint's shared lock on the one snapshot that was read, so a same-directory atomic replacement racing the verification can only yield a self-consistent old or new combination, never a mix of two versions.
73	
74	The optional `--trust-dir PATH` keeps a persistent sequence of the snapshots this machine has accepted, so a whole-bundle replay of an older — otherwise self-consistent — pair is rejected as a rollback. Without the option the single-bundle verification above runs unchanged and no directory is created.
75	
76	The directory carries a lifecycle marker, `state.json`, that leaves exactly one explainable stage after any interruption. When the directory does not yet exist but its parent does, the first verification commits a `"preparing"` state first — binding the bundle's strong tag, the checkpoint byte digest and the candidate node digest — then saves the content-addressed snapshot and node and commits the chain head; the state advances to `"ready"` only after the head commit, and a ready record binds the head digest as well. An interruption in any of those windows is recovered idempotently: the same complete bundle resumes from `preparing` and finishes the sequence, while a bundle carrying a different tag or snapshot is rejected with every staged piece of evidence retained. An existing directory that contains neither a state nor a head — an empty directory, or one holding only unreferenced fragments — is never taken over. A directory from before the lifecycle existed (a legal chain head but no state) is adopted only after its whole chain verifies, and is then stamped ready.
77	
78	With it, the existing verification completes first; then, under the trust directory's exclusive lock, the retained sequence is inspected from its first node to its head on every call: each node digest is recomputed from its strong tag, predecessor tag, checkpoint digest and predecessor node digest; each predecessor digest is followed to a real node whose tag matches; every node's checkpoint snapshot must exist, hit its content address and pass the complete structure and anchor-chain validation; and each pair of adjacent snapshots must satisfy the strict append-only relation below — history continuity is never inferred from node metadata alone. A ready state must also bind the head, the head node and the current snapshot to one another; a missing head or a crosswise relation fails verification. A same-tag replay walks the whole chain just the same, so a corrupted historical node or snapshot cannot be masked by the current bundle. A later bundle carrying the head's strong tag is an idempotent replay: the proof is fully re-verified, the full chain is re-inspected and the directory is left untouched. A new tag is accepted only when its checkpoint is a strict append-only successor of the latest trusted one — existing generations, anchors, fields and values must survive untouched, only new anchors or generations may be appended — so an already retained earlier version, a fork that rewrites old anchors, or a bundle that cannot continue the head fails verification.
79	
80	Each sequence node binds the current tag, the predecessor tag, the checkpoint byte digest and the previous node digest, and the chain head points only at the last complete node, so a restarted process re-checks the real predecessor relation from disk; tampered node content, chain digests, snapshots or head relations are never repaired from the bundle in hand. Directory updates serialize across processes and commit through temporary-file writes, fsync, atomic replace and directory fsyncs, with the head committed before the ready state: any failure keeps the pre-call state, unreferenced complete files are reused on reentry, leftover fragments never take part in any decision, and a content address that already holds different bytes is never overwritten or repaired.
81	
82	On success stdout carries one compact UTF-8 JSON line — `{"valid":true,"etag":...,"generation":...,"closed":...,"events":...,"next":...}` with non-ASCII written through and exactly one trailing newline — the exit status is 0 and stderr stays empty. Failures print no partial stdout, only a single compact failure object on stderr: status 2 `invalid_request` (argument or tag format), 3 `invalid_bundle` (encoding, JSON or structure, including proofs without the snapshot binding and malformed trust metadata), 4 `verification_failed` (tag, digest chain, generation, anchor, predecessor, snapshot, lifecycle-state, page, snapshot-binding or trust-sequence mismatch) and 5 `bundle_unavailable` (missing files, a missing trust-directory parent, or other locking, open or read errors). Failure objects never leak paths, system messages or input content.
83	
84	## Acceptance ledger
85	
86	The `carbon_market.acceptance` module complements the trust directory with a persistent ledger of every bundle submission this machine was offered. `acceptance.submit(checkpoint_path, proof_path, etag, trust_dir, ledger_dir, key)` first runs `audit_proof.verify_bundle` — the complete existing verification, trust-directory sequence included — and records the outcome under the idempotency `key`. Each record carries `key`, `etag`, `checkpoint_digest`, `proof_digest`, `state` and `error` in that order; the `etag` is always the actual strong tag computed from the checkpoint's raw bytes, never the caller's claimed value; `state` is `pending`, `active` or `quarantined`, and `error` names the public exception class only while quarantined.
87	
88	A first submission commits a `pending` record first and only then stores both files' raw bytes content-addressed under the ledger directory, all before verification runs, so an evidence-write failure or a restart resumes the same bundle from the persisted `pending` record instead of posing as never received, and leftover fragments are ignored. Success flips the record to `active` and returns `(record, True)`; a format failure quarantines the record and re-raises `BundleFormatError`, a tag, chain or lifecycle mismatch quarantines it and re-raises `BundleMismatchError` — a claimed tag that does not match the checkpoint's bytes included, and in both cases the evidence stays retained. Replays are idempotent: an `active` record returns its copy with `False`, a `pending` one resumes, a `quarantined` one re-raises the recorded exception type untouched, and the same key with a different bundle retains both bundles' bytes and summaries under `conflicts` (the summary carrying the actual tag as well) without overwriting the main record, raising `ValueError`. The active replay still checks the caller's claimed tag: the identical bundle bytes offered under a tag that does not match the checkpoint's bytes keep their retained evidence, turn the record `quarantined` with `error` `BundleMismatchError` in one atomic commit (a failed commit preserves the old ledger) and raise that same exception — only a replay claiming the correct tag returns the record with `False` and writes nothing. Submissions serialize across processes on the ledger directory's exclusive kernel lock and commit through temporary-file writes, fsync, atomic replace and directory fsyncs; the ledger is one compact UTF-8 `ledger.json` (`version`, `records`, `conflicts`, in that order) ending with a single newline.
89	
90	`acceptance.get(ledger_dir, key)` returns a copy of the record (`KeyError` for an unknown key); `acceptance.search(ledger_dir, cursor=None, limit=100, state=None)` pages the records in key code-point order with a composable state filter and exclusive cursor, returning `{"entries": [[key, record], ...], "next": ...}`. Invalid arguments or an invalid ledger raise `ValueError`, missing inputs or parents `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`.
91	
92	## Acceptance queries
93	
94	```bash
95	python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --audit PATH --auth CONFIG --acceptance DIR
96	```
97	
98	`--acceptance` exposes the acceptance ledger at `DIR` as `GET /acceptance`; it may only be given together with `--audit` and the multi-token `--auth` method — alone, empty, repeated, without `--audit` or paired with the single `--token` it is a usage error (exit status 2) and nothing listens. Without it the path stays a plain 404 like any other unknown path.
99	
100	The same authorization as `GET /audit` applies, in the same order: a missing, blank or duplicated `X-Audit-Token` gets 401 `unauthorized`, an unknown or expired token 403, and an unreadable or invalid configuration 503 `auth_unavailable` — none of these opens the ledger. `GET /acceptance?key=K` looks up one record; the key stands alone, so combining it with `cursor`, `limit` or `state` is 400 `invalid_request`. Without `key` the query paginates with the exclusive `cursor`, the `limit` page size (1..1000, default 100) and the `state` filter, which only accepts `pending`, `active` or `quarantined`; unknown, repeated or empty parameters and illegal values are 400 `invalid_request` as well. Scope checks follow parameter validation and precede any ledger read: an exact lookup requires unrestricted operation and stage scopes and a key scope that is unrestricted or names the requested key, while a paginated query requires all three scopes unrestricted — anything else is a plain 403.
101	
102	A successful exact lookup answers 200 with the record object, a successful page with the `{"entries": [[key, record], ...], "next": ...}` object — both in the library's field order, key code-point order, compact UTF-8 and without a trailing newline. Every 200 response carries a strong `ETag`: one double-quoted string of 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, the SHA-256 of the complete response bytes. The exact lookup and the paginated query each tag their own response bytes, so any visible record, order or cursor change changes the tag.
103	
104	`GET /acceptance` takes an optional `If-None-Match` header: at most one, and only as a single strong tag of that shape. A blank, repeated, weak, wildcard or list conditional is 400 `invalid_request` and never opens the ledger. When the conditional value equals the current snapshot's tag the answer is 304 with an empty body and the same `ETag`; otherwise it is 200 with the full result. The request order is fixed — authorization, query and conditional-header validation, scope checks, and only then the ledger read — and the ledger's shared lock is held from the read through the business-object formation, the response serialization, the digest computation and the conditional comparison, so a request racing a submission decides 200 or 304 from either the complete old ledger or the complete new one, never a mix.
105	
106	The queries only take the ledger's shared-lock read-only path. A missing ledger gets 404 `acceptance_not_found`, an unknown key 404 `acceptance_key_not_found`, an invalid ledger 409 `acceptance_invalid`, and other read failures 503 `acceptance_unavailable`; real paths and system messages never appear in an error.
107	
108	## Migration batch queries
109	
110	```bash
111	python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --audit PATH --auth CONFIG --migration-batches COORD
112	```
113	
114	`--migration-batches` exposes the one fixed migration-batch coordination ledger at `COORD` as read-only `GET /migration-batches` and its incremental change stream at `GET /migration-batches/events`; it may only be given together with `--audit` and the multi-token `--auth` method — alone, empty, repeated, without `--audit` or paired with the single `--token` it is a usage error (exit status 2) and nothing listens. The client can neither pass nor probe any other file path: the ledger is fixed at startup. Without it both paths stay a plain 404 like any other unknown path, and every other interface is unchanged.
115	
116	Authorization is the existing audit authorization and the request order is fixed — identity, query parameters, scope, and only then the ledger read; a failure at one stage never opens a later stage's files. A missing, blank or duplicated `X-Audit-Token` gets 401 `unauthorized`, an unknown or expired token 403 `forbidden`, and an unreadable or invalid configuration 503 `auth_unavailable`. Unknown, repeated or empty parameters and illegal combinations get 400 `invalid_request`. `GET /migration-batches?key=K` returns only that batch's snapshot; the key stands alone, so `cursor` or `limit` beside it is 400, and an unknown batch is a distinct 404 `migration_batch_not_found`. Without `key` the query paginates in ascending batch-key code-point order with an exclusive `cursor` and a `limit` page size (a decimal integer from 1 to 1000, default 100). The page object has, in order, `entries` and `next`; each entry carries, in order, the batch `key`, the complete batch `snapshot` and `completion`. An active batch's `completion` is `null`; a terminal batch's completion is `{"index": i, "at": t}` — the batch's zero-based position in the coordination audit (the real completion order) and its completion moment — so the public completion order and per-item errors are observable. `next` is the key of the page's last entry when more batches remain, else `null`.
117	
118	`GET /migration-batches/events` resumes the incremental progress stream by persisted position: every durable coordination commit that changes an observable batch appends one event, covering batch creation, an ownership takeover after the coordination lease expires, an item's phase transition or saved error, a step receipt landing in the item snapshot, and batch closure. Equivalent replays, coordination-lease renewals and waits on an unchanged plan append nothing. The query takes only an exclusive decimal non-negative-integer `cursor` (omit it to read from position 0; only strictly greater positions are considered), the same 1-to-1000 decimal `limit` (default 100) and optional non-empty string filters `key` (batch key) and `job` (related job id), combined by logical AND; filtered positions never consume page capacity. The page object has, in order, `events` and `next`; each event carries, in fixed order, its strictly increasing zero-based `position` (never reused), the commit moment `at`, the batch `key`, the related `job_id` (`null` for batch-scoped changes), the `category` (`created`, `taken_over`, `item`, `receipt`, `completed`) and the complete post-commit batch `snapshot`. `next` is the page's last position when more matching events remain (it need not match anything itself), else `null`. Unknown or repeated parameters, empty values, a non-decimal `cursor` or an out-of-range `limit` get 400 `invalid_request`. A coordination ledger written before the stream existed keeps loading read-only byte-for-byte and simply yields no events; the first later write upgrades it and seeds one `completed` event per existing audit entry in audit order before appending that run's own events.
119	
120	Scope checks follow parameter validation and precede every file read, using the same records as `GET /audit`: an exact lookup (or a stream query that carries a batch `key`) requires unrestricted operation and stage scopes and a key scope that is unrestricted or names the requested batch, while a cross-batch query — batch pagination or an events query without `key`, even one carrying only a `job` filter — requires the operation, stage and history-key scopes all unrestricted; anything else is a plain 403.
121	
122	The coordination ledger's shared lock together with the nine business ledgers' shared locks covers the ledger reads, the page/snapshot/event formation and the response serialization, so a concurrent batch writer is observed as either the complete old or the complete new version, never a mix; responses are compact UTF-8 JSON with no trailing newline. Before any lock or business ledger is touched, an existing coordination file must first prove its own format — UTF-8, JSON (no negative-zero or non-finite literals), version 1, the fixed field sets and key order and the exact canonical bytes; any such violation raises even when the requested key is absent and is never masked by it. The read never creates the coordination file, a lock file, a directory or any other trace: a miss is decided by an unlocked read before a companion lock file is opened. A missing coordination ledger gets 404 `migration_batches_not_found`; non-canonical content, a broken cross-reference or a referenced business ledger that is missing gets 409 `migration_batches_invalid`; any other read failure gets 503 `migration_batches_unavailable`. Error bodies contain only `error` and never leak a path or system message.
123	
124	The library surface is `migration_batch.get(ledger, key)` (one snapshot, `KeyError` for a missing ledger or unknown key), `migration_batch.search(ledger, cursor=None, limit=100)` (the page object), `migration_batch.events(ledger, cursor=None, limit=100, *, key=None, job_id=None)` (one page of the incremental stream) and the lock-holding `get_response`/`search_response`/`events_response` serializers the endpoint serves. The on-disk ledger gains an optional fourth section, the append-only `events` list in the fixed order `version`, `batches`, `audit`, `events`: baseline ledgers with just the first three sections stay valid and replay byte-for-byte under read-only callers, and the first subsequent write appends the section (seeding it from the audit) in the same atomic commit as any other change.
125	
126	## Resource supply and feasibility
127	
128	The `carbon_market.resources` module complements job acceptance with a persistent, versioned resource-supply registry and a feasibility query over it. `resources.publish(path, resource, idempotency_key)` publishes one supply version: the resource object carries exactly `resource_id`, `region`, `capacity`, `start`, `end`, `unit_cost`, `carbon_intensity` and `residency` — non-empty id and region strings, a positive integer capacity, non-boolean non-negative start, end, unit cost and carbon intensity with start not later than end, and a residency list of distinct non-empty strings sorted by code point that contains the resource's own region. A first publication returns the canonical record — the resource fields plus the next consecutive `version` for that resource id — with `True`, and atomically commits the record, the idempotency binding and a publish audit event binding key, resource id and version. Replaying the same key with an identical resource returns the stored record with `False` and writes nothing; the same key with a different resource, or a new version whose start does not strictly increase over the resource's current latest, raises `ValueError`.
129	
130	`resources.get(path, resource_id, version=None)` reads one record back: the latest version when `version` is omitted, otherwise the exact version. An unknown resource id or version raises `KeyError`.
131	
132	`resources.feasible(job_path, supply_path, job_id, at)` joins a `jobs.submit` acceptance file with the supply file — both read as complete snapshots while their shared locks are held together — and ranks the resources that can serve job `job_id` at the non-boolean non-negative evaluation moment `at`. Each resource contributes only its highest version valid at `at`; a candidate must sit in one of the job's regions, offer at least the job's work as capacity, cover the job's residency regions, and stay available at least until the job's deadline. The total cost is the job's work times the unit cost and the total carbon the work times the carbon intensity; exceeding either budget excludes the candidate. The result is ordered by carbon intensity, then unit cost, then resource id, each entry carrying the resource record and both totals — an empty list when nothing qualifies. A version-1 `jobs.register` file is invalid structure here, and an unknown job id raises `KeyError`.
133	
134	The supply file is one compact UTF-8 JSON document — version, history sorted by resource id and version, idempotency map sorted by key, audit events — with non-ASCII written through and exactly one trailing newline; negative-zero and non-finite number literals are illegal. Every read entry (`publish`, `get` and `feasible`, and any consumer of the supply file) requires the on-disk bytes to be exactly that canonical form: a file whose fields or keys are out of order, which carries any whitespace beyond the structural tokens, which escapes non-ASCII characters, or which misses or doubles the final newline is rejected with `ValueError` just like a malformed or structurally invalid file. Publishing commits under the per-real-path cross-process exclusive lock with pre-call byte restoration on commit failure, queries take the shared lock, and invalid arguments, values, encodings, JSON, structure, ordering, canonical bytes or references raise `ValueError`, missing input files or publish parent directories `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`.
135	
136	## Market clearing
137	
138	The `carbon_market.market.clear(jobs, supply, ledger, job_id, key, at)` entry adds the new-market clearing ledger on top of accepted jobs and the versioned resource supply. The three paths, `job_id` and `key` must be non-empty strings, `at` a non-boolean non-negative integer evaluation moment, and the three paths must resolve to distinct real locations; any violation raises `ValueError` before any business file is read.
139	
140	The acceptance file and the supply file are read as one snapshot under their shared locks, together with the ledger's exclusive lock; the three locks are taken in resolved real-path sorted order so concurrent calls can never deadlock. Only each resource's highest version valid at `at` is considered, and region, residency, cost budget, carbon budget, deadline coverage and the candidate entries (`resource`, `total_cost`, `total_carbon`) follow exactly the `resources.feasible` semantics. In addition, each resource version's capacity is reduced by the work of every trade already booked against that exact resource version in the ledger, so concurrent clearings can never oversell capacity and bookings never cross resource versions. The remaining candidates are ordered by carbon intensity, unit cost and resource id; the first one is the unique winner.
141	
142	The call returns `(trade, created)`. The trade binds the job id, the evaluation moment, the work, the complete ordered candidate snapshot and a versioned selection (`resource_id`, `version`). A missing ledger is created only when the first trade is made; the trade, the idempotency binding (key to job id and evaluation moment) and the audit event binding the request key, the resource id and its selected version are committed together — ledger sections sorted by code point, compact UTF-8 JSON with non-ASCII written through and one trailing newline, written through a synced same-directory temporary file, atomic replace and directory fsync; a failed commit restores the pre-call bytes (or removes a ledger that did not exist).
143	
144	Replaying the same key with the same job and evaluation moment returns the stored trade with `False` without reselecting a resource, appending an event or rewriting a byte. The same key with a changed request, or a job already traded under another idempotency key, raises `ValueError` and leaves the ledger byte-for-byte untouched. An unknown job raises `KeyError` and no remaining feasible resource raises `LookupError`; neither creates the ledger. Missing input files or a missing ledger parent raise `FileNotFoundError` without leaving a ledger or temporary fragment. Invalid ledger structure, references, ordering or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`; other locking, read/write or sync failures raise `OSError`. The existing `market.match`, the `resources` interfaces, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.
145	
146	## Dispatch commitments
147	
148	The `carbon_market.dispatch` module adds the scheduling-commitment layer on top of the clearing ledger, with four persistent, idempotent calls over one dispatch ledger (`version`, `decisions` sorted by job id, `idempotency` and `audit` sorted by key — compact UTF-8 JSON with non-ASCII written through, no negative-zero or non-finite literals, exactly one trailing newline).
149	
150	`dispatch.commit(jobs, supply, trades, ledger, job_id, key, at)` reads the acceptance file, the supply file and the clearing ledger as one snapshot under their shared locks together with the dispatch ledger's exclusive lock, all four taken in resolved real-path order, and creates the job's decision: it binds the traded resource id and version and the job's deadline, and starts `ready` with zero attempts and no owner or lease. The dispatch ledger is created only by this first commit. An unknown job raises `KeyError`, a job without a recorded trade `LookupError`, and a commit moment past the job's deadline `TimeoutError`.
151	
152	`dispatch.claim(ledger, job_id, key, owner, lease, at)` moves a `ready` or `failed` decision to `claimed` under a non-empty owner with a positive integer lease, counting one more attempt; the lease ends at `at + lease` and may not pass the job's deadline. A decision still held under a valid lease, or a lease end beyond the deadline, raises `TimeoutError`. `dispatch.finish(ledger, job_id, key, owner, result, at)` lets the current owner inside its lease record `succeeded` or `failed` and clears owner and lease; a non-claimed decision or an illegal result raises `ValueError`, a different owner `PermissionError`, and a moment past the lease end `TimeoutError`. `dispatch.recover(ledger, job_id, key, at)` returns a decision whose lease has strictly expired to `ready` without counting an attempt; recovering before strict expiry raises `PermissionError`. These three actions take only the dispatch ledger's exclusive lock and fail with `FileNotFoundError` when the ledger does not exist.
153	
154	All four calls return `(decision, created)`; replaying a key with an equivalent request returns the current decision with `False` and writes nothing, while the same key with a different action, job, owner, result, moment or lease raises `ValueError`. Every first-served key commits the decision, the idempotency binding (the complete request) and the audit event (request plus committed decision snapshot) in one synced atomic write that restores the pre-call bytes on failure, so no failed call leaves a half-state. Invalid arguments, nulls, types, structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`, missing inputs or parents `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`. The existing `market.clear`, the `resources` interfaces, the reservation migration, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.
155	
156	## Execution plans
157	
158	The `carbon_market.execution` module adds the recoverable execution layer on top of the dispatch ledger, with three persistent, idempotent calls over one execution ledger (`version`, `plans` keyed by job id and dispatch attempt, `idempotency` and `audit` sorted by key — compact UTF-8 JSON with non-ASCII written through, no negative-zero or non-finite literals, exactly one trailing newline).
159	
160	`execution.plan(jobs, supply, trades, dispatch, ledger, job_id, key, owner, source, at)` reads the acceptance file, the supply file, the clearing ledger and the dispatch ledger as one snapshot under their shared locks together with the execution ledger's exclusive lock, all five taken in resolved real-path order, and creates the plan for one `claimed` decision held by `owner` and still inside its lease — a decision in any other state raises `ValueError`, a different owner `PermissionError`, a moment past the lease end `TimeoutError`. The plan is numbered by the decision's dispatch attempt count and fixes the job, the traded resource id and version, the deadline, the owner and the lease end; one dispatch attempt yields at most one plan. An empty `source` (`None` or `""`) creates a `launch` plan whose steps are `stage` then `start`; a non-empty `source` creates a `migrate` plan whose steps are `copy` then `switch`, and the source must name a published resource other than the target whose residency list covers the job's residency regions, else `LookupError`. A job without a recorded trade raises `LookupError` as well, and an unknown job or decision `KeyError`. The execution ledger is created only by this first plan.
161	
162	`execution.record(ledger, job_id, attempt, key, owner, step, result, receipt, at)` appends one step receipt — the step, `succeeded` or `failed`, a non-empty receipt string and the moment — to an active plan; steps advance only on success, a receipt naming anything but the next pending step raises `ValueError`, a failed step terminates the plan as `failed`, a successful last step as `completed`, and terminal plans accept no further receipts. Only the plan's owner acting inside the lease may record: a different owner raises `PermissionError` and a moment past the lease end `TimeoutError`. `execution.recover(ledger, job_id, attempt, key, at)` turns an active plan whose lease has strictly expired `interrupted`, preserving every recorded receipt; recovering before strict expiry raises `PermissionError`. These two calls take only the execution ledger's exclusive lock and fail with `FileNotFoundError` when the ledger does not exist.
163	
164	All three calls return `(plan, created)` and share one idempotency key space; replaying a key with an equivalent request returns the current plan with `False` and writes nothing, while the same key with a different action, job, attempt, owner, source, step, result, receipt or moment raises `ValueError`. Every first-served key commits the plan, the idempotency binding (the complete request) and the audit event (request plus committed plan snapshot) in one synced atomic write that restores the pre-call bytes on failure. An unknown job or attempt raises `KeyError`; invalid arguments, nulls, types, structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`, missing inputs or parents `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`. The existing `dispatch` interfaces, `market.clear`, the `resources` interfaces, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.
165	
166	## Execution synchronization
167	
168	The `carbon_market.execution_sync` module adds the persistent reconciliation layer on top of the execution and dispatch ledgers with one call, `execution_sync.run(execution, dispatch, ledger, owner, key, now, lease)`. The three ledger paths must be non-empty strings resolving to distinct real locations, `owner` and `key` non-empty strings, `now` a non-boolean non-negative integer moment and `lease` a non-boolean positive integer coordination lease; any violation raises `ValueError` before a business file is read.
169	
170	The first call for a batch `key` scans the execution ledger by job id and attempt and fixes the batch as exactly the terminal plans (`completed`, `failed` or `interrupted`) no earlier batch has already synced. A `completed` plan finishes the dispatch decision as succeeded, a `failed` plan as failed, and an `interrupted` plan recovers the strictly expired claim; the action moment is always history — the last step receipt's moment for a finish, the recorded execution-recovery moment for a recover — and a retry can never rewrite it. Each item is first persisted `pending` in the coordination ledger, and only then is the existing `dispatch.finish`/`dispatch.recover` interface called with an idempotency key derived stably from the batch key and the plan identity, so a crash re-entry replays the very same request. The item becomes `applied` only after a successful call or an equivalent replay, saving the returned decision; a failure records the public exception class, keeps the item pending and re-raises the original exception with its chain.
171	
172	The call returns `(batch, created)`, a fixed-order copy of the current batch snapshot and the first-creation flag. The same batch key fixes its first scan forever: re-entry continues the unfinished items and a completed batch replays without rewriting a byte; terminal plans appearing later require a new batch key, and even an empty first scan commits an explicit `completed` state with the full audit snapshot. An active batch may only be continued by its current owner — a different owner before strict lease expiry raises `PermissionError` — while after expiry another owner may take over without repeating any applied item. Before any advance, the dispatch decision's state, attempt, owner and lease are checked against the plan (as is a dispatch idempotency key already bound to a different request); any mismatch raises `ValueError` without advancing.
173	
174	The coordination ledger (`version`, `batches` sorted by key with each batch's items sorted, and an append-only `audit`) is one compact UTF-8 JSON document with non-ASCII written through, decimal integers and exactly one trailing newline. The coordination ledger's exclusive lock is taken first and held for the whole run, followed by the two input ledgers' shared locks in resolved real-path order — released before the existing dispatch interface takes the dispatch ledger's own exclusive lock per item — so concurrent processes lock in one acyclic real-path order and can never deadlock. Every commit goes through a synced same-directory temporary file, atomic replace and directory fsync; a failed commit restores the previous bytes (or removes a ledger that did not exist) and clears the leftover fragment. Invalid structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`; missing input files or the ledger parent raise `FileNotFoundError`; other locking or I/O failures raise `OSError`. The existing `execution`, `dispatch` and `market` interfaces, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.
175	
176	## Live signal ledger
177	
178	The `carbon_market.signals` module adds an independent ledger of live signals beside the static cost and carbon intensity baked into a resource version. A signal carries exactly `region`, `observed`, `expires`, `mix`, `unit_cost` and `carbon_intensity` — a non-empty region string, non-boolean non-negative observation and expiration moments with the expiration not earlier than the observation, non-negative unit cost and carbon intensity, and a non-empty `mix` object whose values are non-negative integers summing to exactly ten thousand (basis points). Any extra field is rejected.
179	
180	`signals.publish(path, signal, idempotency_key)` publishes one signal version for its region. A first publication returns the canonical record — the signal fields plus the next consecutive `version` for that region, starting at 1 — with `True`, atomically committing the record, the idempotency binding and a publish audit event binding key, region and version. Replaying the same key with an identical signal returns the stored record with `False` and writes nothing; the same key with a different signal, or a new version whose `observed` does not strictly increase over the region's current latest, raises `ValueError` and preserves the original bytes.
181	
182	`signals.get(path, region, at)` returns the region's latest signal observed no later than the non-boolean non-negative evaluation moment `at` and not expired at it (when several windows cover `at`, the highest version wins). An unknown region raises `KeyError`, and no valid version raises `LookupError`.
183	
184	The signal file follows the supply file's exact contract: one compact UTF-8 JSON document — version, history sorted by region and version, idempotency map sorted by key, audit events — with non-ASCII written through, no negative-zero or non-finite literals and exactly one trailing newline, and every read requires the on-disk bytes to be that canonical form. Publishing takes the per-real-path cross-process exclusive lock with pre-call byte restoration on commit failure; invalid arguments, values, encodings, JSON, structure, ordering, canonical bytes or references raise `ValueError`, a missing input file or publish parent `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`.
185	
186	## Live feasibility and clearing
187	
188	`resources.feasible_live(job_path, supply_path, signal_path, job_id, at)` is the dynamic counterpart of `resources.feasible`: the acceptance, supply and signal files are read as one snapshot under their shared locks (the three paths must be distinct real locations). Each resource contributes only its highest supply version valid at `at`; its region, capacity, residency and deadline constraints are unchanged, but the unit cost and carbon intensity are taken from the resource region's latest signal that is valid at `at` rather than from the supply version. A region without a current signal simply removes that resource; it is never an error. The totals, `max_cost`/`carbon_cap` exclusions and the ordering (signal carbon intensity, then signal unit cost, then resource id) follow `feasible`; each result entry carries `resource`, `signal` (the full frozen signal record with its version), `total_cost` and `total_carbon`, and an empty list means no candidate. An unknown job raises `KeyError`.
189	
190	`market.clear_live(jobs, supply, signals, ledger, job_id, key, at)` adds live clearing on top of the same clearing ledger used by `market.clear` — the call takes the three snapshot shared locks and the ledger exclusive lock, all four locked in resolved real-path order, and deducts each booking from the capacity of the exact resource version, counting trades made by either `clear` or `clear_live`, so the two pricing modes share one capacity pool and never oversell. Feasibility follows `resources.feasible_live`: highest valid supply version, latest unexpired region signal driving cost and carbon, the same residency, budget, deadline and ordering rules. The returned trade freezes the ordered candidates, each carrying both its immutable resource version and its immutable signal version, and the selection keeps `resource_id` and `version`; a signal published after the trade can never change it.
191	
192	The replay and conflict rules mirror `clear`: the same key with the same job and evaluation moment returns the stored trade — static or live — with `False` without reselecting, appending an event or rewriting a byte; the same key with a changed request, or a job already traded under another key, raises `ValueError` with the ledger untouched; an unknown job raises `KeyError` and no remaining feasible resource `LookupError`, neither creating the ledger. The ledger keeps the same version 2 canonical form; static trades stay signal-free while live trades carry the frozen signal, so existing `clear`, `dispatch`, `execution` and `execution_sync` readers keep working over a ledger that contains live trades. Invalid structure, references, ordering or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`; missing input files or a missing ledger parent raise `FileNotFoundError`; other locking, read/write or sync failures raise `OSError`. The existing resource, clearing and README public entry points and the HTTP behavior are unchanged.
193	
194	## Re-evaluation and migration advice
195	
196	The `carbon_market.rebalance` module adds the missing re-evaluation layer on top of the live signals, the booked clearing trades and the dispatch and execution layers. `rebalance.evaluate(jobs, supply, signals, trades, dispatch, execution, ledger, job_id, key, at)` re-reads an unfinished booking at the non-boolean non-negative evaluation moment `at` and advises whether the job should keep running on the resource version its trade froze or migrate to a resource whose current version is cleaner or cheaper under the latest signals. The seven paths, `job_id` and `key` must be non-empty strings and the seven paths must resolve to distinct real locations; any violation raises `ValueError` before a business file is read.
197	
198	All seven files are read as one snapshot: the six input files under shared locks and the advice ledger under its exclusive lock, all taken in resolved real-path order. The retained item always uses the exact resource version the trade froze — a newer published version of the same resource never replaces it, even once the frozen version's own supply window would have passed. A migration item uses only another resource's highest supply version valid at `at`, never a different version of the current resource. Every item prices on the region's latest signal observed no later than `at` and not expired at it (a region without such a signal simply drops out), and keeps the job's regions, residency, deadline coverage, cost budget and carbon budget. Capacity is deducted per exact resource version for the trades of every *other* job, while this job's own frozen occupancy is never deducted against itself. Feasible items are ordered by signal carbon intensity, then signal unit cost, then resource id. The first item is the advice target: `keep` when it is still the current resource version, otherwise `migrate`.
199	
200	Advice is refused before any write, in a fixed order: a dispatch decision that has already succeeded, or an execution plan that has already completed, raises `ValueError`; an active execution plan raises `PermissionError` (the booking must not be re-decided while work is in flight); and an evaluation moment past the job deadline raises `TimeoutError`. An unknown job or dispatch decision raises `KeyError`; a job without a recorded trade or an empty feasible set raises `LookupError`; none of these creates the advice ledger. An interrupted or failed plan does not block re-evaluation; the record's `execution` field freezes `none`, `active`, `completed`, `failed` or `interrupted` from the plan with the highest dispatch attempt, and `dispatch` freezes the decision state at evaluation time.
201	
202	The call returns `(record, created)`. The record freezes, in order, `job_id`, `at`, `current` (`resource_id`/`version`), the `dispatch` and `execution` states, the ordered `candidates` (each carrying the frozen resource record, the frozen signal record, `total_cost` and `total_carbon`), the `recommendation` and the `target`. A first evaluation returns the record with `True` and commits it together with one audit event in the advice ledger; replaying the same key with the same job and evaluation moment returns the stored record with `False` without writing a byte, while the same key with a changed request raises `ValueError` and leaves the ledger untouched.
203	
204	The advice ledger (`version`, `records` and `audit` sorted by idempotency key) is one compact UTF-8 JSON document with non-ASCII written through, decimal integers and exactly one trailing newline. Every read requires the on-disk bytes to be that canonical form; the frozen supply and signal references, totals, ordering, the current selection and the keep/migrate target are revalidated against the current snapshots, while the dispatch/execution states stay frozen point-in-time facts. Commits go through a synced same-directory temporary file, an atomic replace and a directory fsync, restoring the pre-call bytes on failure; a failed call leaves neither a temporary fragment nor half an audit event, and a missing ledger parent raises `FileNotFoundError` without creating the ledger. Invalid arguments or ledger bytes raise `ValueError`, other locking or I/O failures `OSError`. The existing `resources`, `market`, `dispatch`, `execution` and `execution_sync` interfaces, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.
205	
206	## Advice execution and re-reservation
207	
208	`rebalance.apply(jobs, supply, signals, trades, dispatch, execution, advice, ledger, job_id, advice_key, key, at)` turns one recorded migration advice into a persisted re-reservation, so the target capacity the advice pointed at is pre-emptively held for the job before any execution plan moves it. The eight paths — the seven snapshots of `evaluate` plus the intent ledger — must be non-empty strings resolving to distinct real locations, `job_id`, `advice_key` and `key` must be non-empty strings and `at` a non-boolean non-negative integer reservation moment; any violation raises `ValueError` before a business file is read.
209	
210	All eight files are read as one snapshot: the seven inputs under shared locks — the advice ledger is now an input — and the intent ledger under its exclusive lock, all taken in resolved real-path order. Only a `migrate` advice recorded under `advice_key` for this very job can be applied: a `keep` advice, an advice key belonging to another job or a reservation moment earlier than the advice moment raises `ValueError`. The booking must be unfinished and not in flight, refused in a fixed order: a succeeded dispatch decision or a completed execution plan raises `ValueError`, a claimed decision or an active execution plan raises `PermissionError`, and a reservation moment past the job deadline raises `TimeoutError` — none of these writes. An unknown job, advice key or dispatch decision raises `KeyError`, and a job without a recorded trade raises `LookupError`; none of these creates the intent ledger.
211	
212	The candidate set is recomputed at `at` under the same rules as `evaluate` — the retained item is the trade's frozen version, every migration item is another resource's highest supply version valid at `at`, each item prices on its region's latest signal valid at `at` and keeps the job's regions, residency, deadline coverage and both budgets — except that capacity is now deducted per exact resource version for every trade *and* every other job's recorded intent, while this job's own source occupancy is never deducted against itself. The advice target must still be the first ordered candidate: a changed target, an empty feasible set or insufficient remaining capacity raises `LookupError` and reserves nothing.
213	
214	The call returns `(record, created)`. The record freezes, in order, `job_id`, `advice_key`, `at`, the `source` and `target` selections (`resource_id`/`version`), the target's frozen `supply` and `signal` records, the `dispatch` and `execution` states and the `reserved` state. A first reservation returns the record with `True` and commits the intent, its idempotency binding and one audit event — the complete request plus the committed intent — in one synced atomic write; replaying the same key with the same job, advice key and moment returns the stored record with `False` without writing a byte, while the same key with a changed request, or a job already reserved under another key, raises `ValueError` and leaves the ledger untouched.
215	
216	The intent ledger (`version`, `intents` sorted by job id, `idempotency` sorted by key and `audit` sorted by key, one binding and one event per intent) is one compact UTF-8 JSON document with non-ASCII written through, no negative-zero or non-finite number literals and exactly one trailing newline. Every read requires the on-disk bytes to be that canonical form; the frozen supply and signal references, the source and target selections, the advice reference and the cross-section bindings are revalidated against the current snapshots, while the dispatch/execution states stay frozen point-in-time facts and capacity stays a decision-time fact. Commits go through a synced same-directory temporary file, an atomic replace and a directory fsync, restoring the pre-call bytes on failure; a failed call leaves neither a temporary fragment nor half an audit event, and a missing ledger parent raises `FileNotFoundError` without creating the ledger. Invalid arguments, structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`; other locking, read/write or sync failures raise `OSError`. The existing clearing, migration advice, dispatch, execution and serving interfaces and the HTTP behavior are unchanged.
217	
218	## Migration claim, execution and release
219	
220	`rebalance.start(jobs, supply, signals, trades, dispatch, execution, advice, ledger, job_id, key, owner, lease_end, at)` closes the loop the reservation opened: it claims one recorded `reserved` intent — neither finished nor already occupied — and freezes the intent's source and target resource versions into a migration plan bound to an `owner` and a `lease_end` that must not pass the job deadline, with the step sequence `copy` then `switch`. The target capacity stays exclusively held by the intent for the whole execution. The eight paths, `job_id`, `key` and `owner` must be non-empty strings resolving to distinct real locations, `lease_end` a non-boolean positive integer and `at` a non-boolean non-negative integer start moment; any violation raises `ValueError` before a business file is read. All eight files are read as one snapshot under the same locking discipline as `apply` — the seven inputs shared, the intent ledger exclusive, all in resolved real-path order.
221	
222	Only an unfinished, unclaimed booking may start a migration, refused in a fixed order: an already `active` plan raises `PermissionError` and a terminal one `ValueError`; a succeeded dispatch decision or a completed execution plan raises `ValueError`; a claimed decision or an active execution plan raises `PermissionError`; and a start moment past the job deadline raises `TimeoutError` — none of them writes. An unknown job, intent or dispatch decision raises `KeyError`.
223	
224	`rebalance.record(jobs, supply, signals, trades, dispatch, execution, advice, ledger, job_id, key, owner, step, result, receipt, at)` lets the current owner, inside the lease, commit the non-empty `receipt` of the next pending step — `copy` then `switch`, never skipped or repeated. A plan that is not active raises `ValueError`, a different owner raises `PermissionError` and a moment past the lease end raises `TimeoutError`. A receipt moment earlier than the plan start or earlier than the previous receipt raises `ValueError`. A successful `switch` turns the plan `migrated` and releases the source capacity the trade froze; any `failed` step turns the plan `failed` and releases the target reservation immediately, leaving the source trade occupancy untouched. Terminal plans accept no further receipts.
225	
226	`rebalance.recover(jobs, supply, signals, trades, dispatch, execution, advice, ledger, job_id, key, owner, at)` turns an active plan whose lease has strictly expired into `interrupted`, preserving every recorded receipt and releasing the target reservation. A plan that is not active raises `ValueError`; a different owner, or a lease that has not expired yet, raises `PermissionError`.
227	
228	The three calls share one idempotency key space with `apply`: replaying a key with the same request returns the current plan snapshot with `False` and writes nothing, while the same key with a changed request raises `ValueError` and leaves the ledger untouched. The first `start` atomically upgrades the intent ledger to the history layout — every recorded intent, idempotency binding, step receipt and audit event is preserved, with intents keyed by their reservation (apply) key and plans keyed by their own start key, and the upgrade lands in the same synced atomic write that creates the first plan rather than waiting for a later reservation. From then on each reservation key locates exactly one intent and each start key exactly one plan: the start request persistently names the reserved intent it claimed (`intent_key`) and every step and recovery request persistently names the plan it acted on (`plan_key`), so an old action key always replays against its own plan and never a later migration round. `record` and `recover` locate their plan by that bound start key; a single-migration ledger written by an older version stays readable, a read-only call or an equivalent replay never upgrades or rewrites a byte, and the first new first-served receipt or recovery upgrades it the same way. `apply` keeps writing the ledger's existing layout — a ledger that has never held a plan stays a version 1 ledger. Capacity accounting recognizes the plan states: a `reserved` or `active` intent occupies both source and target, a `migrated` one only the target, a `failed` or `interrupted` one only the source. Every read requires the same canonical compact form and every commit the same synced atomic replace with pre-call byte restoration as the other ledgers; an unknown job or intent raises `KeyError`, missing input files or the ledger parent raise `FileNotFoundError`, invalid arguments, structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`, and other locking, read/write or sync failures raise `OSError`. The existing `serve`, HTTP and other public interfaces are unchanged.
229	
230	## Terminal settlement and the current binding
231	
232	`rebalance.settle(jobs, supply, signals, trades, dispatch, execution, advice, ledger, settlements, job_id, plan_key, key, at)` turns a terminal migration plan into the job's durable current occupancy in one *independent* settlement ledger — the trade, dispatch, execution, advice and intent ledgers are never rewritten. The nine paths are the eight lifecycle paths plus the settlement ledger; they, `job_id`, `plan_key` and `key` must be non-empty strings resolving to distinct real locations and `at` a non-boolean non-negative integer settlement moment, all checked before a business file is read. `plan_key` is the idempotency key of the `start` request that created the plan. The eight inputs are read as one snapshot under shared locks and the settlement ledger under its exclusive lock, all nine taken in resolved real-path order.
233	
234	Only a terminal plan settles. An `active` plan raises `PermissionError` and creates no record; a missing job, intent or plan, or a `plan_key` that is not the plan's start key, raises `KeyError`. A settlement moment earlier than the terminal evidence — the last step receipt, or the recorded recovery moment for an `interrupted` plan — raises `ValueError`; a legitimate late recovery whose settlement runs past the job deadline is still accepted, so no deadline timeout is enforced. Contradictory terminal evidence, the same key carrying a changed request, another key settling the same migration, a broken running generation or contradictory snapshot references raise `ValueError`.
235	
236	A `migrated` plan confirms the target version as the current occupancy (`active`) and records the source version as the previous-generation binding; a `failed` or `interrupted` plan forms a compensation (`compensated`): the current occupancy stays on the source version and the target reservation stays released. The record freezes, in order, `job_id`, `plan_key`, the continuous running `generation` (the immutable trade is generation 0, the settlement generation 1), the source terminal state `migration`, the `before` and `after` resource selections (`resource_id`/`version`), the settlement moment `at`, the `state` (`pending`, `active`, `compensated`) and `audit` — the sorted, deduplicated idempotency keys of every intent-ledger action the migration committed (reservation, claim, step receipts and recovery).
237	
238	The first request first durably writes `pending` — record, idempotency binding and audit event in one synced atomic write — and only then advances the record to `active` or `compensated` in a second synced atomic write. If the process dies after the pending write, re-entering with the same key and same request resumes the unfinished finalization, completes it and still returns the record with `True`, never repeating a committed occupancy, generation or audit action; the pending bytes are the rollback base for the final write, so a failed finalization leaves a resumable pending settlement rather than restoring the pre-call bytes. Only an already completed same-key same-request call returns the current record with `False` and writes no new byte; the same key with a changed request raises `ValueError` and leaves every file untouched.
239	
240	`rebalance.current(jobs, supply, signals, trades, dispatch, execution, advice, ledger, settlements, job_id)` is a strictly read-only view of the job's latest resource binding for later dispatch and execution: all nine paths are read under shared locks and nothing is created or written. A settled job returns the settlement's current selection — the target version for an `active` settlement, the source version for a `compensated` one — together with its `generation`, `state` and settlement moment; a job without a completed settlement returns the immutable version its trade froze with `generation` 0 and state `traded`. An unknown job raises `KeyError` and an accepted job without a trade raises `LookupError`.
241	
242	The settlement ledger (`version`, `records` and `idempotency` and `audit`, all keyed by idempotency key in code-point order) is one compact UTF-8 JSON document with non-ASCII written through, no negative-zero or non-finite number literals and exactly one trailing newline. Every read revalidates the plan reference, the start association, the before/after selections, the terminal moment ordering and the audit association against the current snapshots. Commits go through a synced same-directory temporary file, an atomic replace and a directory fsync, restoring the pre-call bytes (or the resumable pending bytes) on failure; a missing ledger parent raises `FileNotFoundError` without creating the ledger. Invalid arguments, structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`; other locking, read/write or sync failures raise `OSError`. The existing serving, HTTP and all other public interfaces are unchanged.
243	
244	## Test
245	
246	```bash
247	python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
248	```
249
